title: AI in indie games: do players care as much as developers do?
author: ObjectiveBank1903
selftext:
Hello!  
  
A year ago I started working on a game with no experience or training on gamedev. I always wanted to create a game but I didn't know how to code or do anything artistic but still thought of myself as creative. So I used AI to assist me with my weak points.  
  
Being from Peru I thought I had a unique setting for a simulator game, so I put a lot of effort in recreating it and keeping it as immersive as possible.

My steam page went live a few days back and I found a lot of strong reactions against my game. When I asked for feedback on the mechanics, the immersion, the trailer, the page, all is ignored and the comments target my page's AI use disclosure. 

It made me wonder

How much do you think AI use actually impacts player perception vs. developer perception?

Do players generally care as much as dev communities do, or is this mostly a gamedev-space dynamic?

Curious to read your thoughts.

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body:
You might be exaggerating. I am a dev too and I find ai tools on average mostly useless for any kind of complex work or architecture. If you are working on something very simple they might be effective but otherwise in my experience they make me lose more time than what I can gain. Even VS's code completion tends to waste time as it generates mostly useless stuff. But I am sure it's my fault that I don't know how to use them effectively, right?

The most effective use of a chatbot that I have seen is asking it questions like "what's the best approach / pattern to solve this problem" or super repetitive tasks like parsing a text file. Using AI for anything visual like computer graphics is hopeless.

replies.author: Embarrassed_Split236
replies.body:
Idk what engine you use but AI can do basic things pretty well as long as you tell it what to do in pseudocode, it’s definitely fees faster if you want to make repetitive scriptable objects or you want to go back through multiple scripts and change a pattern of logic or referencing. Not to mention basic refactoring or just getting it to comment/summarize code you haven’t touched in a while.

Obviously (skilled) humans are still better but there’s a reason entry level jobs are getting screwed over by AI, it’s a way cheaper and faster assistant.

replies.author: StickStill9790
replies.body:
This is the crux. You add an extra year of (solo) development time for a demographic that will never buy your product.

replies.author: StickStill9790
replies.body:
My last comment was stricken because a bot thought it was a threat, so to rephrase:

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body:
It adds time only if you wanted to do everything by yourself. Normally a game would be a team effort, where people work in parallel. So if you hire artists, unless they are late with their work you can save time.

What, you won't even invest a bit of your money into your project?

replies.author: StickStill9790
replies.body:
Reality trumps moral outrage.


I’m a graphic designer, and my bill for said work (an entire game’s worth of assets) would be in the tens of thousands. It would take a couple months, but it would be professional and stylish. It would also be far better than anything an AI would regurgitate. I know because I’ve done it.


How many solo developers do you know who have that kind of cash easily available, and quadruple it for sound and music, an x programmer to review the code, and a script writer to go over the massive amountof text required.


ANYTHING that cuts the cost is a blessing, as most people making their game are already working another job and have life obligations.

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body:
Point is, you aren't owed anything.

If it is too expensive, then you don't do it and find another solution. There are plenty:

1. Apply for funding and/or pitch to a publisher.

2. Save up enough money: you don't have to fund an AAA game on your own, you can pay a few assets or enough to have a proof of concept, so that you can then do #1.

3. Change art style to something you are more comfortable with.

4. Take some time to learn how to do it.

5. Team up with other people. You are not forced to do all of it on your own.

Why is running towards AI generation the preferred solution here? Because IMO, it's not. You lose part of the audience and the result is sub-par anyway. So it's a lose-lose situation I'd rather play a text adventure than anything where generative AI assets are front and centre. 

I really don't think genAI is the unexpected boon that will elevate thousands of creatives that were otherwise unable to communicate their genius with us. To me, the only thing it says the person who uses it is lazy.

replies.author: StickStill9790
replies.body:
And those are all valid points, but again they’re all moral points. You want everyone else to participate in your no-AI religion. Why shouldn’t I use this tool? Because a religiously fervent guy might not like it.


AI does not replace artists, or writers. Anyone with talent can see that in a heartbeat. What it does it give a hand to the talentless to raise the bad quality parts of work to mediocre. It puts opportunity into the hands of the poor, that their work can be finished and purchased.


 Hundreds of great text adventures were released last year. How many did you buy?

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body:
> Why shouldn’t I use this tool? Because a religiously fervent guy might not like it.

Certainly not because I said so. It should be you (generic you) to reach that conclusion on your own, because the end result of AI is mediocrity and you should want better for your own creative project.

> It puts opportunity into the hands of the poor, that their work can be finished and purchased.

That's a nice fable, but no sorry. AI subscriptions are paid too. If you want to use a local model, you need a very expensive PC too. Far more than what you would need if you were creating the art or code yourself.

If you want to get political, paying for AI models puts money in the hands of multi-billionaires that don't even give any worth to your life, and helps disenfranchise the poor, funds disinformation and anti-democratic movements across the world.

> Hundreds of great text adventures were released last year. How many did you buy?

I have bought very few games as I am dedicating my free time on my own organically-developed game and learning some art skills too.

As I wrote in another thread, just yesterday I was looking at the gameplay video of a game I was interested in (Solar Expanse). Few minutes in a let's play video on youtube I am greeted with an AI gen video. I immediately lost interest in that game and won't buy it.

replies.author: StickStill9790
replies.body:
Believe me, I don’t want to change your mind. I just don’t like it when people try to force their beliefs on others. Buying a game, writing a review without playing, and then refunding it is evil to me. That’s what is happening now. That’s not voting with your wallet, that’s actively trying to hurt anyone that doesn’t agree with you.


Second I run all my AI stuff off a 600$ computer, no subs, no corps. I train models on my own work, use it for international translation, and use it to write boilerplate code.


It’s a tool.

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body:
> Buying a game, writing a review without playing, and then refunding it is evil to me.

Never done anything of that sort. Now that I think about it, I have never refunded anything from steam. But well, there are consumer protection laws anyway. 

> That’s not voting with your wallet, that’s actively trying to hurt anyone that doesn’t agree with you

Everyone is free to change their minds for whatever reason, not necessarily because of AI. I personally if I know the game is heavily genAI-based I'd rather not buy it to begin with.

But you have to assume a certain % of people will refund your game. If you want to appeal to the truly anti-AI militant user groups, then well you know what to do and not do.

> I train models on my own work

You train, as in, completely new models? Do you have your own Qwen-like model available? All that on a 600$ pc, wow!

replies.author: StickStill9790
replies.body:
Yes, it takes forever and it can’t be used for final work, but yes I have my own custom made models. I don’t use any of the large models since they overload my memory, but I have small tight models designed for very specific output. 


Turns out that having taken tens of thousands of photos over the years, plus a service that quantified all the data categorically, is more than enough to teach a small model basic functions.


This is the same way hospitals train AI to spot liver disease in a blood teat or diabetes by the sound of your voice. It’s not AI, but machine learning, that is useful.


Granted, not everyone can do all that. Which is why we have public models.

replies.author: Lethandralis
replies.body:
You misunderstand me I think. What I mean is say you have 10 reviews a day after launch. A single "AI Bad therefore this game is bad" review can drop your steam score from e.g. Positive to Mixed. This has a massive impact on the organic impressions steam allocates to your game.

Since marketing tends to have a snowballing effect, this is something to consider.

It definitely does hurt a game, even if the bad reviews are for petty reasons.

Meaning don’t market it being AI until after you have a player base.

comments.author: josh_the_dev
comments.body:
TLDR: Visible obvious AI will likely lower sales.

First an foremost people care about quality. Unfortunately it's hard to see and so they have to judge on a first glance (couple of screenshots). Now AI lowered the barrier of entry for making games leading to more crappy games. Has nothing to do with ai directly just that now inexperienced people are able to publish a game. People associate certain things with low effort and by extension bad quality. AI art is one of these things.

There are also a few people who hate AI for other reasons and will specifically not buy something made with AI. That's mostly because it's such a dividing topic at the moment.

comments.author: Am_Biyori
comments.body: Players care about fun. A game doesn't have to be overly original or unique, but it does have to give the play a feeling of a unique experience. At the moment that's hard to do with AI alone. So many "prototypes" are put out as finished or nearly finished games that most people will think of them when they hear AI. For those using AI as their first line of defense there needs to be a stronger commitment to taking the quality level up a notch and also to encourage others to do the same.

comments.author: Disastrous-Entity-46
comments.body:
the game market  is highly saturated. i think that its very hard to stand out with any game. 

that said, i think the question is always one of quality and user experience. game dev is the craziest field- some amazing, classic games are created by a single guy or a dedicated team of a few people.  but also, huge studios release games that can flop, or buggy messes that may get redeemed in the future (or not).

i think there are legitimate concerns about the use of ai. but i also think that its a difficult market to get attention in these days, and gamers often feel like ai development is the new "asset flip "- the sign of someone not putting efffort into a game, just trying to make a quick buck.

comments.author: Sweaty-Counter-1368
comments.body:
The problem is “who” cares. Most people don’t actually care…. But the people who care are the more chronically online, engaged players… that you want on your side or neutral, definitely not against you.

So they overrepresent in online spaces, set the sentiment, shout out the Reddit and can actively ruin things that help build community. They create a hurdle where you basically need to create something great, not good, to overcome it.

Black Ops 6 had a record breaking launch and is the best selling PS5 game in the U.S., Crimson Desert has almost 50k reviews with an estimate of over 2m copies sold....literally nobody cares except people on art and indie dev subs when the bad guys are big corpos, not Joe Blow solo developer.

I think my point wasn't clear.

Players don't care. The loud majority on Indie dev and art subs do, which almost certainly aren't your target audience anyway.

replies.author: shlaifu
replies.body: no? I had the impression indie games largely succeed on the buzz they create in the indie scene, which includes these groups. (of course, with exceptions of HUGE successes like Expedition 33 or Vampire survivors, which managed to transcend the indie realms)

Posting on indie dev and art subs is unlikely to be the representative of your primary audience for your indie game. Just because someone develops an indie game does not mean they would be an automatic wishlist for \*your\* indie game.

replies.author: shlaifu
replies.body:
I didn't mean other indie devs are the *primary* customers. I just mean they are part of the crowd, and they function as multipliers.
I mean, they obviously do, as OP just learned. Definitely at least for anti-AI sentiment.

comments.author: alphapussycat

As long as it's not noticeable players won't care, they won't read the AI disclaimer. If you put it in the short discription and scream at people in your forum, like some guy here did, they will care. 

They might care, they just simply won't investigate, so they just won't know.

comments.author: TechnicaGames
comments.body:
Let the game speak for itself.   
  
What's the different if a dev use arts entirely from free asset packs? Since he didn't 'made' it himself for may be the lacks of artistic skill or the time or whatever reasons. How is that different from using AI generated arts? Then what about some game that make arts by human artists but turns out that art pieces are 'derivative' works from other artists? What's the difference? What about computer graphic in general? Special effects in the blockbuster movie? Does 'human' create it by hands? 

I'm fully agree that craftsmanship should be praised, but that also should be when it is the main consideration. Art competition, Game award, Art schools - that's the place. 

For business world, any means to ship quality product within budget and time should be considered valid - as long as it's ethical. As long as the game turn out to be good and fun without violating anyone's right - it is a Good game.

comments.author: Apoptosis-Games

For the most part, players don't care at all.

As always, other devs will be your worst enemy
